highlights.content: [BUSINESS](https://www.globaltimes.cn/business/index.html) / [ECONOMY](https://www.globaltimes.cn/business/economy/index.html) Chinese tech company unveils new AI model based on fully domestic computing power By Zhang Weilan Published: Oct 22, 2026 08:59 PM iFlytek 1024 Global Developer Festival 2026 is held in Beijing on October 22, 2026. Photo: Zhang Weilan/Global Times Chinese tech company iFlytek released and open-sourced its general-purpose large-language model (LLM), Spark-X2.6, at an industry event in Beijing on Thursday. The new model is an end-cloud integrated LLM that the company said has achieved breakthroughs in coding and agentic capabilities using fully domestic computing infrastructure. The model, sized at 293-A30B mixture-of-experts architecture (293B total parameters, 30B active per token), supports a context window of 1 million tokens and has been deployed on a domestic 10,000-card inference cluster.  "Spark-X2.6 has taken the lead in breaking through the efficiency bottleneck of long-horizon task training on domestic chips, truly achieving independence and controllability with homegrown computing power," the company's chairperson Liu Qingfeng said at the iFlytek 1024 Global Developer Festival 2026 held in Beijing on Thursday. The company said that the model has reached performance levels comparable to leading industry systems in multiple technical benchmarks. However, Liu emphasized that the model's real-world deployment performance in actual industrial scenarios — such as state-owned enterprises, education, healthcare and judicial services — outperforms its public benchmark scores. An industry observer attending the event told the Global Times that the emphasis is shifting away from sheer model size and benchmark competition toward deployment on domestic computing, data security, and real-world usefulness in office, industrial and research settings.  Liu Dingding, a veteran industry analyst, said that the combination of end-cloud collaboration and a fully domestic hardware base offers a reference path for China's artificial intelligence (AI) industry. "What matters next is whether a model can be rooted in a domestic computing foundation, balance efficiency with data security, and truly enter real scenarios of office work, industry and scientific research," Liu noted. The development also comes as ties between Chinese AI modelmakers and domestic chip suppliers deepen. According to domestic media reports, a research team led by the Shenzhen Loop Area Institute in South China's Guangdong Province has successfully used Huawei's Ascend 910C chips to complete post-training for the DeepSeek-V4-Pro model, marking a major step forward as China's semiconductor industry tries to leap from supporting basic AI inference to more complex model training. Liu said that tighter US restrictions on AI chip exports to China are increasing the strategic importance of domestic computing infrastructure, adding that closer collaboration between model developers and domestic chipmakers is pushing China's AI ecosystem from "usable" to "practical" and more mature. Our Tests Show Big Improvements But Humans Remain Key * [AI](/tag/ai) * [Geolocation](/tag/geolocation) * [LLMs](/tag/llms) *Sign up [here](https://bellingcat-investigations.beehiiv.com/) to receive Bellingcat’s biggest investigations by email as soon as they are published*. In September, the AI company Anthropic published a blog post that claimed its models were approaching “[superhuman capabilities](https://www.anthropic.com/research/intelligence-targeting-conventional-weapons-capabilities) for geolocating outdoor photos”. Anthropic made this claim by comparing its models’ performance to that of players of the popular online game GeoGuessr, which challenges users to geolocate Google Street View images. Bellingcat has been running its own benchmark tests on AI [models](https://www.bellingcat.com/resources/how-tos/2025/06/06/have-llms-finally-mastered-geolocation/) since June 2025, right around the time when Large Language Models (LLMs) began to challenge reverse image searches for assisting with geolocation tasks. In our first round, GPT 4o-mini from OpenAI appeared to be the best tool for geolocating, a title which was taken by Google AI mode when we performed [our second round](https://www.bellingcat.com/resources/2025/08/14/llms-vs-geolocation-gpt-5-performs-worse-than-other-ai-models/) of tests a few months later in August 2025. This time, we significantly upped the ante for the models, providing increasingly challenging photos and asking for only one set of coordinates. We tasked not only closed-weight models from [Claude](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/overview), [Grok](https://docs.x.ai/developers/models), [Gemini](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/models), [ChatGPT](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models), and [Mistral](https://docs.mistral.ai/models), but also [open-weight](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-definitions/what-is-an-open-weight-model) models from Moonshot AI’s [Kimi](https://platform.kimi.ai/docs/models), commercial provider [GeoSeer](https://geoseeer.com/) and the non-generative geolocation model [GeoClip](https://github.com/VicenteVivan/geo-clip). In total, we fed each model 52 photos that had not been published anywhere on the internet before. The results showed that the current generation of models have markedly improved geolocation capabilities. Anthropic’s Opus and Fable, as well as Google’s recent Gemini 4 Argon model, performed the best on geolocation tasks, narrowing down locations from images faster than a human could under specific conditions. Preliminary tests of a set of agentic skills and tools being developed internally by Bellingcat also showed promising results in further improving the geolocation performance of generic-use AI agents. But crucially, the tests also showed why humans remain necessary for accurate and trustworthy geolocation work, as no models were foolproof. This is particularly important given the increased use of AI in military contexts. The Anthropic blog post focused specifically on geolocating photos for military and intelligence purposes such as targeting, a historically labour-intensive process requiring significant human expertise. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Reduck Secures $3M to Cut AI Agent Web Tasks 3x [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Oct 22, 2026 · 16 min read A French-American startup called Reduck has raised $3 million in a pre-seed funding round to solve a problem that has quietly become one of the biggest bottlenecks in agentic AI: what happens when the website an AI agent needs to use has no API. The round, reported by [Tech.eu](https://tech.eu/2026/10/22/reduck-secures-3m-to-make-web-automation-faster-for-ai-agents/) on October 22, 2026, was led by Daphni, with participation from Drysdale Ventures and Galion.exe. The money is going toward a product called Reduck MCP, a platform that lets AI agents discover, execute, and even create browser-automation scripts on their own, without an engineer wiring up a traditional API integration first. The timing matters. Over the past year, AI agents have moved from chatbot demos to systems that book travel, file expense reports, scrape competitor pricing, and manage CRM records on a company’s behalf. Nearly all of that work depends on software talking to other software through APIs. But most of the internet still does not expose a clean API, and a lot of enterprise software locks its most useful functions behind login screens and custom web interfaces. Reduck is betting that the gap between “agents that can reason” and “agents that can actually click buttons on a website” is where the next wave of AI infrastructure spending will land. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Reduck Actually Builds: Inside the Reduck MCP Platform Reduck’s core product, Reduck MCP, is built around the Model Context Protocol, the open standard that lets AI models call external tools in a structured way. Instead of asking a developer to write and maintain a custom integration for every target website, Reduck MCP gives an AI agent a library it can search, a way to execute an existing automation, and a way to generate a brand-new one when nothing suitable exists yet. According to the Tech.eu report, that library already contains more than 1,200 ready-to-run automation scripts spanning over 250 websites, which means an agent calling Reduck MCP is often reusing work that has already been built, tested, and hosted rather than improvising from scratch on every request. Reduck’s own site lists use cases that illustrate the idea in practice, including [building a company list and enriching it with funding and news](https://reduck.ai/use-cases/research-startups-and-funding) pulled straight from the web rather than a paid data API. That “discover, execute, create” loop is the part Reduck is pitching as its differentiator. Most browser-automation tooling built for AI agents today still asks a human to define the workflow up front: click here, type there, wait for this element to load. Reduck flips that order. The agent decides what it needs to accomplish, searches Reduck’s hosted library for a matching automation, runs it if one exists, and if nothing matches, the agent itself produces a new automation script that Reduck then hosts and executes going forward. AI Agents.titleZh: Reduck Secures $3M for AI Agent Web Automation
AI Agents.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Reduck Secures $3M to Cut AI Agent Web Tasks 3x [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Oct 22, 2026 · 16 min read A French-American startup called Reduck has raised $3 million in a pre-seed funding round to solve a problem that has quietly become one of the biggest bottlenecks in agentic AI: what happens when the website an AI agent needs to use has no API. The round, reported by [Tech.eu](https://tech.eu/2026/10/22/reduck-secures-3m-to-make-web-automation-faster-for-ai-agents/) on October 22, 2026, was led by Daphni, with participation from Drysdale Ventures and Galion.exe. The money is going toward a product called Reduck MCP, a platform that lets AI agents discover, execute, and even create browser-automation scripts on their own, without an engineer wiring up a traditional API integration first. The timing matters. Over the past year, AI agents have moved from chatbot demos to systems that book travel, file expense reports, scrape competitor pricing, and manage CRM records on a company’s behalf. Nearly all of that work depends on software talking to other software through APIs. But most of the internet still does not expose a clean API, and a lot of enterprise software locks its most useful functions behind login screens and custom web interfaces. Reduck is betting that the gap between “agents that can reason” and “agents that can actually click buttons on a website” is where the next wave of AI infrastructure spending will land. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Reduck Actually Builds: Inside the Reduck MCP Platform Reduck’s core product, Reduck MCP, is built around the Model Context Protocol, the open standard that lets AI models call external tools in a structured way. Instead of asking a developer to write and maintain a custom integration for every target website, Reduck MCP gives an AI agent a library it can search, a way to execute an existing automation, and a way to generate a brand-new one when nothing suitable exists yet. According to the Tech.eu report, that library already contains more than 1,200 ready-to-run automation scripts spanning over 250 websites, which means an agent calling Reduck MCP is often reusing work that has already been built, tested, and hosted rather than improvising from scratch on every request. Reduck’s own site lists use cases that illustrate the idea in practice, including [building a company list and enriching it with funding and news](https://reduck.ai/use-cases/research-startups-and-funding) pulled straight from the web rather than a paid data API. That “discover, execute, create” loop is the part Reduck is pitching as its differentiator. Most browser-automation tooling built for AI agents today still asks a human to define the workflow up front: click here, type there, wait for this element to load. Reduck flips that order. The agent decides what it needs to accomplish, searches Reduck’s hosted library for a matching automation, runs it if one exists, and if nothing matches, the agent itself produces a new automation script that Reduck then hosts and executes going forward. Readers who have set up tool-calling infrastructure themselves can get a feel for the plumbing involved by looking at how [Cursor’s MCP server setup](https://shattered.io/set-up-cursor-mcp-servers-2026/) or a [secure MCP server built for Claude](https://shattered.io/build-secure-mcp-server-claude-2026/) handles tool discovery, since both follow the same protocol family Reduck is building on top of. ## The No-API Problem That’s Slowing Down Agentic AI Reduck’s pitch rests on a specific technical complaint, and...

LLMs.titleZh: Chinese tech company unveils new AI model based on fully domestic computing power - Global Times
LLMs.content: [BUSINESS](https://www.globaltimes.cn/business/index.html) / [ECONOMY](https://www.globaltimes.cn/business/economy/index.html) Chinese tech company unveils new AI model based on fully domestic computing power By Zhang Weilan Published: Oct 22, 2026 08:59 PM iFlytek 1024 Global Developer Festival 2026 is held in Beijing on October 22, 2026. Photo: Zhang Weilan/Global Times Chinese tech company iFlytek released and open-sourced its general-purpose large-language model (LLM), Spark-X2.6, at an industry event in Beijing on Thursday. The new model is an end-cloud integrated LLM that the company said has achieved breakthroughs in coding and agentic capabilities using fully domestic computing infrastructure. The model, sized at 293-A30B mixture-of-experts architecture (293B total parameters, 30B active per token), supports a context window of 1 million tokens and has been deployed on a domestic 10,000-card inference cluster.  "Spark-X2.6 has taken the lead in breaking through the efficiency bottleneck of long-horizon task training on domestic chips, truly achieving independence and controllability with homegrown computing power," the company's chairperson Liu Qingfeng said at the iFlytek 1024 Global Developer Festival 2026 held in Beijing on Thursday. The company said that the model has reached performance levels comparable to leading industry systems in multiple technical benchmarks. However, Liu emphasized that the model's real-world deployment performance in actual industrial scenarios — such as state-owned enterprises, education, healthcare and judicial services — outperforms its public benchmark scores. An industry observer attending the event told the Global Times that the emphasis is shifting away from sheer model size and benchmark competition toward deployment on domestic computing, data security, and real-world usefulness in office, industrial and research settings.  Liu Dingding, a veteran industry analyst, said that the combination of end-cloud collaboration and a fully domestic hardware base offers a reference path for China's artificial intelligence (AI) industry. "What matters next is whether a model can be rooted in a domestic computing foundation, balance efficiency with data security, and truly enter real scenarios of office work, industry and scientific research," Liu noted. The development also comes as ties between Chinese AI modelmakers and domestic chip suppliers deepen. According to domestic media reports, a research team led by the Shenzhen Loop Area Institute in South China's Guangdong Province has successfully used Huawei's Ascend 910C chips to complete post-training for the DeepSeek-V4-Pro model, marking a major step forward as China's semiconductor industry tries to leap from supporting basic AI inference to more complex model training. Liu said that tighter US restrictions on AI chip exports to China are increasing the strategic importance of domestic computing infrastructure, adding that closer collaboration between model developers and domestic chipmakers is pushing China's AI ecosystem from "usable" to "practical" and more mature. Our Tests Show Big Improvements But Humans Remain Key * [AI](/tag/ai) * [Geolocation](/tag/geolocation) * [LLMs](/tag/llms) *Sign up [here](https://bellingcat-investigations.beehiiv.com/) to receive Bellingcat’s biggest investigations by email as soon as they are published*. In September, the AI company Anthropic published a blog post that claimed its models were approaching “[superhuman capabilities](https://www.anthropic.com/research/intelligence-targeting-conventional-weapons-capabilities) for geolocating outdoor photos”. Anthropic made this claim by comparing its models’ performance to that of players of the popular online game GeoGuessr, which challenges users to geolocate Google Street View images. Bellingcat has been running its own benchmark tests on AI [models](https://www.bellingcat.com/resources/how-tos/2025/06/06/have-llms-finally-mastered-geolocation/) since June 2025, right around the time when Large Language Models (LLMs) began to challenge reverse image searches for assisting with geolocation tasks. In our first round, GPT 4o-mini from OpenAI appeared to be the best tool for geolocating, a title which was taken by Google AI mode when we performed [our second round](https://www.bellingcat.com/resources/2025/08/14/llms-vs-geolocation-gpt-5-performs-worse-than-other-ai-models/) of tests a few months later in August 2025. This time, we significantly upped the ante for the models, providing increasingly challenging photos and asking for only one set of coordinates. We tasked not only closed-weight models from [Claude](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/overview), [Grok](https://docs.x.ai/developers/models), [Gemini](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/models), [ChatGPT](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models), and [Mistral](https://docs.mistral.ai/models), but also [open-weight](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-definitions/what-is-an-open-weight-model) models from Moonshot AI’s [Kimi](https://platform.kimi.ai/docs/models), commercial provider [GeoSeer](https://geoseeer.com/) and the non-generative geolocation model [GeoClip](https://github.com/VicenteVivan/geo-clip). In total, we fed each model 52 photos that had not been published anywhere on the internet before. The results showed that the current generation of models have markedly improved geolocation capabilities. Anthropic’s Opus and Fable, as well as Google’s recent Gemini 4 Argon model, performed the best on geolocation tasks, narrowing down locations from images faster than a human could under specific conditions. Preliminary tests of a set of agentic skills and tools being developed internally by Bellingcat also showed promising results in further improving the geolocation performance of generic-use AI agents. But crucially, the tests also showed why humans remain necessary for accurate and trustworthy geolocation work, as no models were foolproof. This is particularly important given the increased use of AI in military contexts. The Anthropic blog post focused specifically on geolocating photos for military and intelligence purposes such as targeting, a historically labour-intensive process requiring significant human expertise. LLMs.content: SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 22, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- The research explores advances in LLM training, adaptive reasoning, and reinforcement learning. Ten papers involving researchers from MemoraX AI’s founding research team and its academic and industry collaborators have been accepted to the 2026 Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), one of the leading international conferences in artificial intelligence and machine learning. The research spans large language model (LLM) post-training, inference optimization, adaptive reasoning, and online reinforcement learning. Across these areas, the work explores how AI systems can learn more reliably, allocate computational resources more effectively, and make better decisions in complex environments. NeurIPS 2026 will take place December 6–12 in Sydney, Australia, with satellite events in Atlanta, Georgia, and Paris, France, from December 9–13. Advancing AI Learning, Reasoning, and Decision-Making As AI agents take on increasingly complex and long-running tasks, researchers face fundamental challenges: making model training more reliable, aligning training objectives with actual inference performance, allocating reasoning resources more effectively, and developing robust decision-making strategies for complex environments. MemoraX AI is building next-generation AI memory infrastructure while pursuing research in memory modeling, reinforcement learning, and agent systems. Its research explores how memory can move beyond information storage and retrieval to become a learnable capability that helps agents retain context, manage information, and apply accumulated experience to future tasks. The company’s work spans text memory, work and coding memory, and multimodal memory. For developers building AI applications, Memory API supports memory writing, search, updates, and deletion. MemoraX Code, the company’s persistent-memory tool for coding agents, helps agents retain repository structure, architectural decisions, coding preferences, and debugging experience across sessions and agents. The underlying technical challenge is how to make memory itself learnable, enabling systems to determine what to retain, when to update or retrieve information, and how to turn historical interactions into reusable experience. Four Representative Papers Four representative papers from the NeurIPS 2026 selections illustrate different approaches to improving AI learning, reasoning, and decision-making. 1. Beyond Correctness: Robustness-Driven Evolutionary Self-Training for Large Language Models Research focus: LLM post-training and reasoning reliability A correct answer does not necessarily indicate a reliable reasoning process. This paper introduces TREST, a robustness-driven evolutionary self-training framework that evaluates the stability of reasoning paths under sampling perturbations and prioritizes more robust trajectories for training. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, TREST achieved an average accuracy of 49.83%, outperforming the GRPO and Iterative RFT baselines in the reported experiments. The work offers an approach to improving the reliability of LLM reasoning by considering not only whether a solution is correct, but also whether the reasoning strategy remains effective under variation. 2. The Mirage of Optimizing Training Policies: Monotonic Inference Policies as the Real Objective for LLM Reinforcement Learning Research focus: Reinforcement learning and inference optimization Improvements during training do not always translate into better performance when a model is deployed. This paper examines inconsistencies between training and inference in LLM reinforcement learning, where improvements in a training policy may not translate into better performance from the policy used at inference time. The tool aims to help developers detect behavior changes in large language model APIs.* **Martingale introduces Raven Alpha for model drift detection** PALO ALTO, US — October 22, 2026 — Martingale, a data infrastructure and analytics company focused on artificial intelligence, announced on Tuesday the launch of Raven Alpha, a novel method for detecting drift in AI models. The company said Raven Alpha ranks first among model drift detection approaches in independent evaluations. The announcement was made by co-founders Arjun Hans, Veenu Damarla, and Jayden Ishihara, who are computer science students at Carnegie Mellon University. ![A blue, geometric origami bird flies across a black background, representing the Raven Alpha model.](https://prnow.io/uploads/press-releases/Codex_Image_Sep_24_2026_11_14_57_PM_mvjrd6ue_61069ea1.jpg) ![A blue, geometric origami bird flies across a black background, representing the Raven Alpha model.](https://prnow.io/uploads/press-releases/Codex_Image_Sep_24_2026_11_14_57_PM_mvjrd6ue_61069ea1.jpg) Model drift occurs when an AI model’s behavior changes over time, often due to updates or shifts in underlying data. For developers building products on large language model APIs from providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic, undetected drift can cause applications to fail or produce inconsistent results. Martingale’s method is designed to identify such changes before they affect end users. **Founders combine academic research with practical focus** Hans, Damarla, and Ishihara developed Raven Alpha while studying at Carnegie Mellon. According to the company, the team’s approach outperforms established drift detection techniques in head-to-head comparisons. The founders have not disclosed the specific benchmarks used, but they said the results have been validated through internal testing and will be submitted for peer review. Martingale is positioning Raven Alpha as a tool for enterprises and developers who rely on third-party AI APIs. The company said the method can be integrated into existing monitoring pipelines and provides early warnings when model behavior deviates from expected patterns. **Early access and availability** Raven Alpha is currently available in a limited early access program. Martingale plans to release a commercial version later this year, with pricing to be announced. The company said it is working with several design partners to refine the product and gather feedback from production environments. The launch comes as businesses increasingly depend on AI models for critical functions, raising the stakes for reliability and consistency. Martingale’s entry into the drift detection market adds a new option for organizations seeking to maintain oversight of third-party AI systems. **About Martingale** Martingale is a data infrastructure and analytics company specializing in AI model monitoring and drift detection. AI Product.content: IT Brief New Zealand - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief New Zealand logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg) New Zealand](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.co.nz) ![AI tool sprawl leaves US executives facing orchestration gap](https://itbrief.co.nz/uploads/story/2026/10/22/dan-gardner-story-322131.webp) [Digital Transformation](https://itbrief.co.nz/tag/digital-transformation) [CX](https://itbrief.co.nz/tag/customer-experience) [ERP](https://itbrief.co.nz/tag/enterprise-resource-planning) # AI tool sprawl leaves US executives facing orchestration gap Fri, 23rd Oct 2026 (Today) [![Mara Sugue](https://itbrief.co.nz/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTg1OSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--c35d782a2ad379dbb3ebd1d7a0269b918cf68f7f/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/maraheadshot.webp) MARA SUGUE News Editor](/author/mara-sugue) Research from Code and Theory and WSJ Intelligence shows that 85% of C-suite executives say their AI technology stacks are disconnected. The study surveyed 801 senior executives at US companies with annual revenue of at least USD $500 million. The findings suggest many large businesses are struggling to turn heavy investment in artificial intelligence into measurable returns. Companies use an average of 183 AI tools, the research found, yet most lack the systems needed to connect them, even though 94% of respondents say better orchestration is essential to growth. The report describes this as an orchestration gap between adopting AI tools and operating as a connected enterprise. It also suggests senior management increasingly expects AI projects to produce financial results, with 85% of respondents saying AI must now deliver a measurable return on investment. At the same time, many executives said the spread of AI software has created new problems inside organisations. Three in five said tool proliferation had left strategic execution stagnant, while two-thirds said their organisations regularly uncover redundant AI investments. **Ownership issues** The research also points to uncertainty over who is responsible for connecting AI systems across the business. It found that 42% of Chief Executive Officers believe they own AI orchestration, while 57% of technology leaders say the same. One in four companies said no one is clearly accountable. The split suggests governance remains unsettled as companies move from experimentation to broader deployment. The study also found that only 18% of organisations apply the same governance and accountability standards to AI agents as they do to human leaders. **Structural barriers** Executives said the biggest obstacles were organisational rather than technical. Siloed mindsets and corporate culture were cited by 61%, followed by fragmented data and incompatible data models at 58%, the absence of a centralised operating layer at 56%, skill gaps at 38% and budget constraints at 29%. Customer-facing operations also appear to be affected. The survey found that 78% of executives said customer channels lack a unified data model and brand architecture, indicating that fragmentation extends beyond internal systems into front-end operations. According to the report, only 15% of AI investments currently operate as a unified system with shared intelligence across the organisation. More than two-thirds of companies have not issued a request for proposal for a centralised orchestration system, suggesting many have yet to formalise a response. The study focused on executives at larger US companies, a group likely to have extensive software estates and multiple AI projects running in parallel. Wuhan Zhiyue Chuangda Technology adopts the dual-engine architecture of "Intelligent Central Base + AI Development Framework", which shortens the delivery cycle of enterprise customized AI systems from several months to one week. At present, its products have expanded from the development platform to desktop terminals, all-in-one machines and C-end scientific research applications. In July 2025, Wuhan Zhiyue Chuangda Technology Co., Ltd. launched ZAI (Zero to AI), an enterprise-level one-stop AI agent development platform. According to the team, enterprises can complete the development and launch of business intelligence based on this platform in as fast as only one week. Tang Shengwu, founder of Zhiyue Chuangda, has 15 years of experience in the IT industry, and has served as architect, technical director, senior engineer and other positions. The core team is composed of a number of technical experts from well-known technology enterprises. The project started technical R&D in January 2025. The team spent half a year polishing the first version and continued to iterate afterwards. At present, it has completed the layout on four product lines: B-end platform, desktop office, software-hardware integration and C-end scientific research assistant. ## **I. Three Thresholds for Enterprise AI Implementation: Technology, Cost and Security** The capabilities of large models have been rapidly popularized in the past three years, but on the enterprise side, there is still a considerable gap between "being able to use AI" and "using AI well". The founder of the team summarized the common difficulties faced by enterprises into three points: First, the technical threshold is high. An available agent involves multiple links such as model invocation, knowledge base construction, tool orchestration, permission and security. It is difficult for enterprises without AI engineering experience to connect these links on their own. Second, the implementation cycle is long. The traditional customized development from demand sorting to system launch is often calculated in months, which cannot meet the timeliness requirement of business. Third, it is difficult to balance cost and security. Building a self-owned team requires large investment, while standardized SaaS products are difficult to match the personalized business processes and private data requirements of enterprises. As a result, many enterprises' AI attempts remain at the single-point pilot stage and are difficult to enter the core business process. "Either spend a lot of money on self-development, or make do with general products". This mismatch is exactly the market gap targeted by Zhiyue Chuangda's ZAI platform. ## **II. AI Product.content: SecurityBrief Australia - Technology news for CISOs & cybersecurity decision-makers [![SecurityBrief Australia logo](/brands/sb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.com.au) ![Palo Alto Networks launches Cortex XDR One for AI agents](https://securitybrief.com.au/uploads/story/2026/10/23/secure-laptop-phone-network-hub-endpoint-threat-containment-story-322210.webp) [Malware](https://securitybrief.com.au/tag/malware) [Network Security](https://securitybrief.com.au/tag/network-security) [Cloud Security](https://securitybrief.com.au/tag/cloud-security) # Palo Alto Networks launches Cortex XDR One for AI agents Fri, 23rd Oct 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://securitybrief.com.au/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) Palo Alto Networks has launched Cortex XDR One, a platform that combines endpoint detection and response with protection for autonomous AI agents. The product is intended to address risks emerging as businesses allow AI agents to interact with internal systems such as databases, production code, financial ledgers and customer management platforms. Cortex XDR One brings together extended detection and response and Cortex Agentic Endpoint Security in a single interface and sensor. It is designed to cover threats aimed at both traditional operating systems and AI-driven tools used on enterprise endpoints. The launch reflects a broader shift in corporate security priorities as AI coding agents, copilots, Model Context Protocol servers and personal AI tools become more common in day-to-day operations. Palo Alto Networks says these systems can inherit user permissions and act in non-deterministic ways, creating openings for prompt injection, indirect data poisoning and unauthorised API calls. Traditional endpoint detection and response tools were not built to manage those risks. Basic software containers also do not fully address the problem when AI agents can access sensitive systems and data through legitimate credentials. **Platform design** The platform offers real-time visibility into AI software installed on endpoints, including unauthorised tools sometimes described as shadow AI. It also includes execution controls intended to apply checks at both the AI runtime layer and the operating system layer. The product uses small language models on the sensor itself to inspect and block fileless threats even when a device is offline. By processing data locally, organisations can examine suspicious activity without moving sensitive code to the cloud. Another element is a single sensor that gathers telemetry across endpoint activity. Palo Alto Networks says this allows security teams to connect attack chains across different domains, reduce false positives by up to 95%, and support automated remediation. Customers can deploy the agentic endpoint security element as a standalone module alongside third-party endpoint detection and response tools, or use it through the full Cortex XDR One platform. The offer can also be paired with Unit 42 managed detection and response services, which now include managed agentic endpoint security. **AI security focus** The technology behind Cortex Agentic Endpoint Security comes from Palo Alto Networks' integration of Koi, a startup focused on agentic security. The tools were first used internally by the company's information security team before being incorporated into the broader platform. Open Source AI.title: Hugging Face’s New AI Biology Model Lets You Chat With DNA | WIRED
Open Source AI.titleZh: Hugging Face’s New AI Biology Model Lets You Chat With DNA | WIRED
Open Source AI.content: # Hugging Face’s New AI Model Lets You Chat With DNA The AI platform Hugging Face on Thursday released a new open model for understanding DNA that can run locally on a laptop. Developed in collaboration with researchers at Zhongguancun Academy in China and the University of Naples Federico II in Italy, the model is trained on genomic sequences and natural language so that people can ask questions about the effects of DNA changes on gene activity and health and get conversational answers in return. Lewis Tunstall, a senior research scientist at Hugging Face, says the tool is meant to help researchers design new drugs and genetic therapies, and it could potentially aid patients in interpreting their own genomes. “We've unlocked a new capability in language models, which is fundamentally about being able to chat with DNA,” he says of the new model, dubbed Carbon-X. Using natural language means even nontechnical users “can actually ask questions about DNA that wouldn't be accessible through any other tool.” Known as essentially GitHub for AI models, Hugging Face provides a library of readymade AI tools and a platform for running primarily open-weight and open-source AI applications for developers, researchers, businesses, and people who want to experiment with AI without building everything from scratch. In September, Nvidia agreed to acquire the company for nearly $13 billion. (Hugging Face was also at the center of a major hack by OpenAI’s models earlier this year.) DNA is more like computer code than natural language. Instead of 0s and 1s, though, it uses As, Cs, Gs, and Ts to encode information. A human genome contains 6 billion of these letters. While the human genome has been sequenced end to end, scientists still don’t understand how most of it works. Now, AI models are helping researchers decipher some of those mysteries. Last year, Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome, which predicts the effects of DNA sequences and genetic mutations but does so in a numeric format. It also requires more compute power. Evo 2, a model developed by the Arc Institute and Nvidia, along with academic partners, speaks the language of DNA and can generate entire genomes from scratch. Carbon-X integrates both DNA and natural language in a conversational interface. Think of it like a ChatGPT for DNA. The team started with an existing language model and expanded its vocabulary to read DNA in groups of six letters. They then continued training on 300 billion chunks of data, or tokens, that combined DNA sequences, English text, and examples linking DNA to biological descriptions. The DNA sequences came from mammals (including humans), other vertebrates, invertebrates, plants, fungi, and protozoa. Tunstall says the team didn’t train the model on viruses because they didn’t want it to be used for potentially dangerous applications. Users won’t be able to upload full human genomes. The model was trained to be able to ingest DNA sequences of roughly 50,000 base pairs, so users will only be able to query small parts of the genome at a time. One of the ways scientists could use Carbon-X is to help understand whether a genetic mutation is benign or disease-causing, a key step in developing a targeted drug or genetic therapy. If an intervention targets the wrong mutation, it could be totally ineffective or, worse, cause unintended harm. Researchers face restrictions when it comes to uploading identifiable or sensitive patient data to frontier AI models, so Tunstall says his team intentionally designed a small model with 14 billion parameters. That will allow it to run locally on the user’s hardware, rather than rely on cloud-based models. No data is sent to Hugging Face or any other company, he says. The developers of Carbon-X caution that they haven’t validated the model yet with actual wet lab experiments, so they can’t say how accurate its predictions are.

By **[Shittu Olumide](https://www.kdnuggets.com/author/shittu-olumide)**, Technical Content Specialist on October 22, 2026 in [Artificial Intelligence](https://www.kdnuggets.com/tag/artificial-intelligence) --- Google Research has open-sourced **[Harness²](https://github.com/google-research/harness2)** (or **Harness2**), a framework that lets AI agents improve themselves without retraining the underlying model. Open Source AI.titleZh: A malicious program that steals passwords was found embedded in the AI tool 'LiteLLM,' and simply installing it could affect other Python programs as well. - GIGAZINE
Open Source AI.content: # A malicious program that steals passwords was found embedded in the AI tool 'LiteLLM,' and simply installing it could affect other Python programs as well. [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/22/litellm-backdoor/00_m.jpg)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/22/litellm-backdoor/00.jpg) It has been discovered that version 1.107.0 of 'LiteLLM,' an open-source tool that allows users to easily utilize multiple AI models, contained malicious software designed to steal passwords and other sensitive information. The malicious software was designed to run simply by launching Python in an environment where LiteLLM was installed, and it also had the capability to allow attackers to remotely execute other programs. **Compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 on PyPI Installs a Credential Stealer and Backdoor - Real-time Open Source Software Supply Chain Security** [https://safedep.io/litellm-pypi-compromise-credential-stealer-backdoor/ ![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/22/litellm-backdoor/snap9653_m.png)](https://safedep.io/litellm-pypi-compromise-credential-stealer-backdoor/) **Contained: Oct 21, 2026 LiteLLM release v1.107.0 Compromised | liteLLM <https://docs.litellm.ai/blog/security-incident-oct-21-2026>** LiteLLM is a tool that allows you to use various AI models provided by OpenAI, Anthropic, and others through a common mechanism. Because it can unify the connection methods that differ for each AI model, it is used for developing applications that combine multiple AI services. [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/22/litellm-backdoor/01_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/22/litellm-backdoor/01.png) LiteLLM is also available on the Python Package Index (PyPI), a service for publishing and distributing packages for the programming language 'Python'. Developers can install LiteLLM from PyPI, but version 1.107.0, released on October 21, 2026, contained malicious files. According to an investigation by security firm SafeDep, the malicious program was included in all seven packages distributed for Windows, macOS, and Linux. However, the source code published in LiteLLM's official GitHub repository did not contain any malicious files, confirming a discrepancy between the legitimate development code and the contents of the actually distributed packages. The malicious program consisted of three files: 'cook.pth,' 'cook.py,' and 'sitecustomize.py.' Python has a mechanism to automatically load certain configuration files and programs when it starts up, and the attacker exploited the '.pth' file that is loaded when Python starts up to automatically execute 'cook.py,' which steals information. In other words, the malicious program would be executed simply by starting Python in the same environment, even without using LiteLLM. [![](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/22/litellm-backdoor/snap9652_m.png)](https://i.gzn.jp/img/2026/10/22/litellm-backdoor/snap9652.png) The information-stealing program was designed to collect passwords and browsing history stored in the browser, private keys used for SSH connections, and authentication information for cloud services. Furthermore, authentication information for AI development tools such as Claude Code, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot, as well as API keys for AI services managed by LiteLLM, were also targeted. The collected information was encrypted and then sent to an external server called 'www.litellm.dev'. The encryption method used was one in which the attacker possessed the secret key, making it difficult to easily identify the stolen information even if the communication content was examined. Furthermore, 'sitecustomize.py' also contained a backdoor that allowed the attacker to remotely execute the program. The backdoor activated when Python started and continued processing in the background. Every hour, it would check files on GitHub to obtain the target server, re-execute the information-stealing program, and download and execute another program prepared by the attacker. Infra & Chips.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # NVIDIA OpenShell Pins AI Agents to 4 Silicon Layers [2026] ![Priya Anand](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/panand.webp) [Priya Anand](https://shattered.io/author/panand/) Updated Oct 23, 2026 · 16 min read NVIDIA announced the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture on October 21, 2026, at GTC Berlin, and the [Digital Watch Observatory covered the launch a day later](https://dig.watch/updates/nvidia-openshell-architecture-ai-agent-security). The pitch is simple. Build, contain, observe and enforce safe AI agents with controls that live in the infrastructure, not only inside the model. This is a hardware story as much as a software one. NVIDIA ties its open-source OpenShell runtime to Vera Rubin infrastructure, Vera CPUs, BlueField-4 DPUs and a trio of edge systems. Each piece gets a job. Models think on one layer, agents act on another, and a separate layer judges whether the action was allowed. We covered the enforcement piece earlier in our report on [NVIDIA Sentry on BlueField-4](https://shattered.io/nvidia-sentry-bluefield-4-secure-ai-agents-runtime-2026/), and this article widens the lens to the full reference design. Some headlines frame the launch as a fix for agents going rogue. That phrasing is a headline characterization. NVIDIA’s own description centers on four verbs: build, contain, observe and enforce. This piece sticks to what the announcement and the coverage actually confirm, flags what remains open, and offers analysis clearly labeled as ours. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture: What Was Announced The NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture is a blueprint, not a single product you install. NVIDIA describes it as a way to build, contain, observe and enforce safe agents across enterprise infrastructure and edge systems. It rests on NVIDIA OpenShell, the secure runtime software that NVIDIA describes as an open-source runtime enforcing policy-based security, network and privacy guardrails for autonomous agents. The announcement landed on October 21, 2026. According to the Digital Watch Observatory, the reference architecture is available immediately, and NVIDIA says a broad range of technology providers, cybersecurity companies and enterprise software developers are working with it or integrating support for it. NVIDIA did not name those partners in the material we reviewed, so we do not name them either. The full-stack components NVIDIA listed are NVIDIA Vera Rubin infrastructure for model inference, NVIDIA Vera CPUs for agent harnesses and tool use, NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs running NVIDIA Sentry for in-silicon enforcement, and NVIDIA RTX Spark, NVIDIA DGX Spark and NVIDIA DGX Station for edge deployments. That is a lot of product names for one announcement. The design idea behind them is easy to state, though. Do not trust the agent to police itself. Pricing is the obvious gap. NVIDIA did not state a price for the architecture or any component in the cited material. Anyone budgeting for a deployment will have to wait for partner quotes or direct conversations with NVIDIA sales. ## The Full Stack: Four Layers, Seven Named Components The easiest way to read the announcement is as a layer cake. The bottom layer supplies compute for models. The next layer runs the agent logic. A third layer watches and enforces policy. The fourth layer pushes the same ideas onto desks and edge sites. The table below lays out each component and the role NVIDIA gave it. | Layer | Component | Role in the architecture | | --- | --- | --- | | Runtime software | NVIDIA OpenShell | Open-source secure runtime enforcing policy-based security, network and privacy guardrails | | Model infere...

Infra & Chips.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) ![](https://img.youtube.com/vi/e-56iKSx1X4/hqdefault.jpg) [Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e-56iKSx1X4) GuestErik Bernhardsson 4 hours ago01:26:17en ![](/images/img_default_profile@2x.png)[Latent Space](/podcast?source=Latent%20Space) ## Key Takeaways Modal CEO Erik Bernhardsson explains how the AI compute platform aggregates demand across ~25 clouds and pre-sells GPU capacity to serve fast-growing sandbox workloads, arguing that renting beats buying GPUs as hardware prices decline. ## Summary Erik Bernhardsson, co-founder and CEO of Modal, argues that AI infrastructure is entering a new era that cannot be served by wrapping the previous generation of cloud tools — Kubernetes, Docker, and steady-state autoscaling were built for cheap CPUs and flat workloads, not expensive GPUs and bursty inference. Over the course of the conversation he explains how Modal grew roughly 50x in revenue and usage since his last appearance about two years ago, how the company now rents capacity from almost 25 clouds, and why he thinks the industry's habit of selling GPUs in "three-year rectangles" is mismatched to how most customers actually consume compute. The episode is mostly about capacity economics, the two-product structure of Modal (Functions and Sandboxes), and how agents are reshaping both developer experience and internal engineering practice; the "rectangles" framing in the title is one thread among several rather than the organizing subject. Bernhardsson is unusually well positioned to talk about this: he built Spotify's first music recommendation system over roughly seven years starting around 2008–2009, released the open-source Luigi workflow orchestrator, spent five years as CTO of Better.com growing its tech team from two or three people to 300–400, and has been building Modal since 2021. The reader should come away with a concrete picture of the GPU capacity market as seen from a mid-sized infrastructure vendor — who captures the scarcity rent, why neoclouds can scale faster than Modal, and what tail risks Bernhardsson is deliberately hedging against — plus a clear view of where he thinks the next product markets are (training, batch, low-latency voice, post-training) and why he remains a "cloud maximalist" on the on-prem question. ## Capacity is the binding constraint, and the market has shifted from spot to multi-year prepaid deals Bernhardsson says capacity procurement has become one of his three biggest pre occupations, and the structure of the market has changed materially over the past year. In Modal's first few years, almost all capacity came from hyperscaler spot and on-demand instances — initially AWS, then GCP and Azure, with Oracle added early because it offered good rates on A100s and H100s. Spot worked because preemptible capacity could be aggregated across hundreds of regions into one pool. Since then, he says, "in order to get the capacity we need, we have to work with a much larger set of clouds" — almost 25 at this point — and many deals now require three-plus-year commitments with meaningful upfront payments. That has made Modal "slightly less capital efficient" than it once was and forced the company to build a procurement function of about four full-time people plus an engineering team of roughly ten managing bare-metal capacity worldwide, dealing with network issues, bad drives, and "GPUs falling off the bus." | Dimension | Earlier model (through roughly end of 2025) | Current model (as of late 2026) | | --- | --- | --- | | Primary capacity source | Hyperscaler spot and on-demand | Mix of spot, reservations, and 25+ clouds | | Contract structure | Short-term, preemptible | Three-plus-year deals, often prepaid | | Capital efficiency | Very high | Lower; large cash flow needed for...
